steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Leadership is a central theme: Caesar presents himself as the ideal Roman general — decisive, brave, and always in control. Contrast this with Tacitus's portrait of weak or tyrannical emperors.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Roman imperialism: Caesar justifies conquest as bringing civilisation and order to barbarians; Tacitus questions whether empire brings freedom or oppression.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Virtus (manly courage/excellence) is a key Roman value: in Caesar it means military bravery; in Cicero it means moral courage to defend the Republic.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Pietas (duty to gods, country, and family) drives Roman heroes but can also create conflict: duty to the state vs personal loyalty.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is virtus and how does its meaning differ between Caesar and Cicero? | Q: How does Caesar portray the Gauls in De Bello Gallico? | Q: What is pietas and why is it important in Roman culture?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Virtus means manly courage or excellence. In Caesar, it primarily means military bravery and leadership. It is a core Roman value that governs behaviour: Aeneas embodies pietas by putting duty to his mission above personal desire.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always link themes to specific passages in the set text — themes must be supported by textual evidence, not discussed in the abstract. When discussing a theme, show how different authors treat it differently: Caesar celebrates imperialism; Tacitus questions it. Use the Latin terms (virtus, pietas, libertas) rather than English equivalents — it shows deeper understanding of Roman values. For higher marks, discuss how themes interact: virtus serves both leadership and imperialism; pietas can conflict with libertas.
